CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom in the Persian Gulf after a roughly two-month lull in fighting.
After issuing an alert about the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks."

,

A pedestrian walks in front of a Nvidia sign outside the company's headquarters on Nov. 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, Calif. after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board of directors allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," wrote Huang in a statement posted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."

item.title: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
item.description:
I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
November 17, 20266:00 AM ET
By
Mara Gordon
Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to: thrive@npr.org.
Question: My doctor has started recording our office visits with an artificial intelligence scribe. She says it helps write notes in my medical record. I said yes when she asked if I was comfortable with it, but in hindsight I feel a little freaked out. Should I be worried about AI listening in on my private medical conversations?
Answer: AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Doctors are using them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.
I admit I've been an eager adopter in my own primary care practice. I use an app on my phone that records my conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record.
Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR
It saves me time. But more importantly, I like using it because it helps me focus more fully on my patient. When I use the AI scribe, I don't have to talk and take notes at the same time – I can actually make eye contact with my patient rather than staring at the computer screen.

item.description:
Work
She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades
Updated November 17, 20268:28 AM ET
Originally published November 17, 20265:00 AM ET
Andrea Hsu
Ashley Baukman is an apprentice at The Electrical Trades Center in Columbus, Ohio. With the future of work uncertain, some college graduates are turning to the skilled trades for job security.
Andrew Spear for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Andrew Spear for NPR
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
COLUMBUS, Ohio — A few miles south of The Ohio State University, Ashley Baukman is wrestling with a piece of steel tubing, using only a manual tool called a foot pedal and her sheer strength to bend it 90 degrees.
This class in conduit bending at The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio is part of an apprenticeship program Baukman began in the spring. She's here in class one day out of every two weeks. Other days, she's out on construction sites, working under the supervision of journeymen electricians.
For the 36-year-old college graduate and social worker, it's a new chapter — one she hopes will be the foundation of a long-term career.
